title: Google re:Work, A guide to structured interviewing for better hiring practices
text:
## Structured interviewing: Google's four aspects

Google's structured interviewing approach has four core aspects: using vetted, high-quality questions that are relevant to the role; recording comprehensive feedback of candidate answers so evaluators can easily review responses; scoring with standardized rubrics so all reviewers have a shared understanding of what good looks like; and providing interviewer training and calibration so interviewers are confident and consistent.

## Why structured beats unstructured

Structured interviews are more predictive of job performance than unstructured interviews, established by comparing interview scores to the later performance scores of those hires across functions and levels. Pre-made, high-quality questions, guides, and rubrics also save on average 40 minutes per interview. Rejected candidates who received structured interviews reported 35% higher satisfaction than those who did not, so the structure improves the candidate experience even for people who are not hired.

## The three hiring attributes

Google assesses three attributes. Role-related knowledge is probed with behavioral prompts ("Tell me about a time...") that surface how the candidate actually operated. Problem solving is probed with hypothetical scenarios ("Imagine if...") to see analytical reasoning, not just the right answer. Leadership measures initiative and how the person navigates a team, with differentiated expectations for individual contributors versus managers.

## Question and rubric design

Effective questions pair an initial prompt with predetermined follow-ups, and the aim is to assess the quality of reasoning rather than whether the candidate lands on one correct answer. Rubrics define performance levels (poor, borderline, solid, outstanding) with illustrative examples of each, and interviewers record comprehensive notes so evaluation is consistent across candidates.

## Anti-pattern

The classic mistake is the unstructured "free chat" interview where every interviewer asks different questions and scores on gut feel: it predicts job performance far less well, invites bias, and gives candidates an inconsistent experience.

title: Google re:Work, Set goals with OKRs
text:
## What OKRs are

Objectives and Key Results (OKRs) is a goal-setting method popularized at Intel by Andy Grove and adopted at Google. Objectives are ambitious and may feel somewhat uncomfortable. Key results are measurable and should be easy to grade with a number. Grove's two foundational questions frame it: "Where do I want to go?" gives the objective, and "How will I pace myself to see if I am getting there?" gives the key results.

## The numbers

Set 3 to 5 objectives per cycle, each with roughly 3 key results. Grade key results on a 0 to 1.0 scale where 1.0 means full achievement. The sweet spot for a grade is 60 to 70 percent (0.6 to 0.7). If someone consistently scores 1.0, their OKRs are not ambitious enough. Company-level annual OKRs are set first, then teams and individuals cascade quarterly OKRs from them.

## Principles

Transparency: OKRs are public so everyone in the organization can see what others are working on. Stretch: targets should be ambitious, sometimes uncomfortable, with teams expected to reach about 70 percent. Outcomes over activities: key results should describe impact and what is achieved, not the how.

## Anti-pattern: OKRs are NOT performance reviews

A key rule is that OKRs are not synonymous with employee evaluations and should not be used as comprehensive individual assessments. If OKRs are tied to pay and promotion, people sandbag them, setting easy targets they know they can hit 1.0 on, which destroys the stretch mechanism. Keep OKRs about the company's goals and each person's contribution, and run performance evaluation separately.

title: Gallup, The 12 Elements of Great Managing (Q12 employee engagement)
text:
## The Gallup Q12 engagement items

Gallup's Q12 measures the conditions that drive employee engagement. The twelve items are:
1. I know what is expected of me at work.
2. I have the materials and equipment I need to do my work right.
3. At work, I have the opportunity to do what I do best every day.
4. In the last seven days, I have received recognition or praise for doing good work.
5. My supervisor, or someone at work, seems to care about me as a person.
6. There is someone at work who encourages my development.
7. At work, my opinions seem to count.
8. The mission or purpose of my company makes me feel my job is important.
9. My associates or fellow employees are committed to doing quality work.
10. I have a best friend at work.
11. In the last six months, someone at work has talked to me about my progress.
12. This last year, I have had opportunities at work to learn and grow.

## Selected business outcomes tied to specific items

Gallup links each item to hard outcomes. Q1 (clear expectations) associates with 22% turnover reduction, 29% fewer safety incidents, 10% higher productivity. Q3 (do what I do best) associates with 30% turnover reduction, 11% higher profitability, and 36% fewer safety incidents. Q5 (someone cares about me) associates with 46% fewer safety incidents and 41% lower absenteeism. Q11 (talked about my progress) associates with 38% fewer safety incidents and 11% higher profit. Q12 (learn and grow) associates with 39% lower absenteeism and 14% higher productivity.

## Anti-pattern

Q10, "I have a best friend at work," is the item leaders most often want to cut because it feels unserious, but it predicts performance and Gallup keeps it for that reason. The larger anti-pattern is surveying engagement once a year and doing nothing with the results: a measurement with no manager follow-up erodes trust rather than building it.

title: SHRM, Using Behavioral Interviewing Techniques to Select the Right Employees
text:
## Behavioral interviewing: past behavior predicts future performance

SHRM's core premise is that past behavior predicts future performance: applicants tend to repeat previous work patterns in new roles. Behavioral interviews therefore ask for specific examples from a candidate's actual work history rather than hypothetical answers or self-labels like "I'm a people person."

## The process

1. Identify the performance criteria essential for the role, drawn from the job description or a competency list.
2. Design questions that target those specific competencies.
3. Require candidates to give concrete examples from previous experience.

For a customer service role, SHRM lists competencies such as energy, oral communication, stress tolerance, adaptability, customer service orientation, and teamwork. Sample behavioral questions include: "Describe a time when you had to work at a fast pace for a long period," "Describe a time when you had difficulty communicating with a customer," and "Describe a situation in which you were faced with a large amount of customer requests." A structured interview builds questions from job competencies, which most organizations define but few actually align their interviews to.

## Business impact and coaching

Proper hiring reduces turnover cost, which SHRM notes can range from $10,000 to half of an employee's annual salary per replacement. Interviewers should expect to coach candidates during the interview, because most applicants are not used to giving specific examples of their performance.

## Anti-pattern

Asking only hypothetical or leading questions ("You'd handle an angry customer well, right?") lets candidates tell you what you want to hear and gives no evidence of real behavior.

title: Amy C. Edmondson, Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams (ASQ, 1999)
text:
## The founding study of psychological safety

Amy Edmondson's 1999 paper introduced team psychological safety, defined as a shared belief held by members of a team that the team is safe for interpersonal risk taking. In a psychologically safe team, members feel able to speak up, ask questions, admit mistakes, and propose ideas without fear of being embarrassed or punished.

## Model and key finding

The paper tests a model in which psychological safety and team efficacy influence learning behavior, which in turn drives team performance. The primary finding: team psychological safety correlates significantly with learning behavior, whereas team efficacy does not once psychological safety is controlled for. Learning behavior is the mediating pathway, meaning safety matters because it enables the behaviors (seeking feedback, sharing information, experimenting, discussing errors) that ultimately produce results. Both formal team structures (context support, leader coaching) and shared psychological beliefs shape outcomes together.

## Method

The research was a multimethod field study of 51 work teams in a manufacturing company, combining survey instruments with direct observation, and measuring antecedents, process variables (learning behavior), and performance outcomes.

## Why it matters for HR

Psychological safety was later identified in Google's Project Aristotle as the single most important dynamic of effective teams. For HR this reframes "team building": the lever is not personality mix but whether people believe it is safe to take interpersonal risks. Note the common misreading: psychological safety is not lowered standards or being nice. Edmondson pairs high safety with high accountability; safety without standards produces a comfort zone, not a learning zone.

title: Dr. John Sullivan, Google's Simple Just-in-Time Checklist Improves Onboarding Results by 25%
text:
## The just-in-time onboarding checklist

Google emails a hiring manager a short reminder the Sunday before a new hire starts, listing five actions:
1. Have a role and responsibilities discussion.
2. Match your new hire with a peer buddy.
3. Help your new hire build a social network.
4. Set up onboarding check-ins once a month for the new hire's first six months.
5. Encourage open dialogue.

## The result

The checklist reduced time to productivity by 25 percent faster, equivalent to cutting about one full month off the ramp-up period.

## Why timing and design matter

Delivery on the Sunday before the start date is deliberate: it reaches managers exactly when their sense of urgency peaks, rather than weeks in advance when the information gets forgotten. Sullivan draws six principles from it: just-in-time alerts command attention through immediacy; voluntary compliance beats mandates for manager buy-in; brevity and scannable formats maximize adoption; data-driven experimentation proves what works; checklists outperform narrative instructions for busy managers; and team-level onboarding (owned by the manager) outperforms centralized corporate programs for productivity impact.

## Anti-pattern

Generic, HR-owned, day-one paperwork dumps delivered far ahead of time get ignored. Onboarding that ends after the first week also underperforms: Google's structure runs monthly check-ins through the first six months.

title: Forbes (Zack Friedman), Google Says The Best Managers Have These 10 Qualities (Project Oxygen)
text:
## Project Oxygen: the 10 behaviors of great managers

Beginning in 2008, Google researchers set out to understand what makes a manager great at Google, analyzing performance data, surveys, and awards. The result, Project Oxygen, distilled the behaviors of the best managers. The list, later expanded from eight to ten, is:
1. Is a good coach (invests time to coach and shares best practices).
2. Empowers the team and does not micromanage (gives space and flexibility).
3. Creates an inclusive team environment, showing concern for success and well-being.
4. Is productive and results-oriented.
5. Is a good communicator, listens and shares information.
6. Supports career development and discusses performance.
7. Has a clear vision and strategy for the team.
8. Has key technical skills to help advise the team.
9. Collaborates across Google.
10. Is a strong decision-maker (prioritizes action over endless analysis).

## What it teaches HR

The striking finding was that technical skill ranked last of the eight original behaviors: what employees valued most were coaching, empowerment, and clear communication, not the manager being the smartest engineer in the room. Google used these behaviors to build manager feedback surveys and training, turning research into a repeatable development program rather than a poster on the wall.

title: SHRM, Introduction to the Inclusion and Diversity Discipline (BEAM Framework)
text:
## Definitions

SHRM defines inclusion as structures that enable every employee, regardless of role or background, to contribute, be heard, and succeed based on merit and performance. Diversity is reflecting a wide range of backgrounds and identities. Legally compliant inclusion and diversity means initiatives that promote equal opportunity and fairness without favoring or excluding anyone based on a protected characteristic.

## The BEAM Framework (Belonging Enhanced by Access through Merit)

Five pillars: Inclusion (opportunities open to all without regard to protected status); Access for All (initiatives that engage talent without regard to protected status); Merit-Driven (opportunities based on job-related qualifications, skills, knowledge, or performance); Inclusive and Accessible Information (initiatives communicated clearly and consistently through inclusive channels); and Skills-First Optimization (supporting skill-building so all eligible people can improve their qualifications).

## Business case with numbers

Organizations in the top quartile for workforce diversity were 39% more likely to outperform on financial expectations (McKinsey 2023). Four-fifths of workers surveyed in August 2024 by The Conference Board supported their organization's inclusion and diversity efforts, and two-thirds said they would not work for a company that dismissed them.

## Ten-step implementation

Identify business objectives; compile workforce and market data; assess gaps; secure executive buy-in with a business case; audit existing policies; establish missing policies; check legal compliance using BEAM; implement and communicate; measure impact; then review and calibrate. Legal safeguards include working with legal from the outset, using structured interviews and pay-equity audits, and monitoring federal, state, and local regulation.

## Anti-pattern

Headcount-only diversity scorecards (counting bodies without measuring hiring, development, promotion, and retention across the pipeline) and initiatives that favor or exclude by protected status create legal risk and can backfire.

title: Deel, How Google Runs Performance Reviews (calibration and the two conversations)
text:
## Calibration

Google finalizes performance ratings through calibration: five to ten managers meet to discuss their draft ratings and agree on final scores before anything is shared with employees. As Laszlo Bock explained, calibration removes the pressure managers feel from employees to inflate ratings and diminishes bias by forcing managers to justify their decisions to one another. No rating is final until calibration concludes. Managers draft ratings based primarily on OKRs plus contextual factors, on a scale of Needs Improvement, Consistently Meets Expectations, Exceeds Expectations, Strongly Exceeds Expectations, and Superb.

## Separate the feedback and pay conversations

Google deliberately holds the development-feedback conversation and the compensation conversation about one month apart. Bock's rule: never have the pay and feedback conversations at the same time. Combining them kills learning, because when money and status are on the line people become defensive and stop absorbing feedback. Separating them keeps the feedback purely qualitative and actionable.

## Anti-pattern

The most common performance-management mistake is exactly what Google engineered against: a single annual meeting that mixes the rating, the raise, and the developmental feedback. When those collide, employees hear only the number and the pay, and the coaching is lost. Uncalibrated solo ratings also drift, some managers grade generously and some harshly, which is unfair across teams.

title: Schmidt & Hunter (1998), The Validity and Utility of Selection Methods (course outline)
text:
## The canonical validity ranking of hiring methods

Schmidt and Hunter's 1998 meta-analysis summarized 85 years of personnel-selection research and reported the validity (correlation with later job performance) of the major selection methods:

- General Mental Ability (GMA): r = .51
- Work sample tests: r = .54
- Structured interview: r = .51
- Unstructured interview: r = .38
- Integrity tests: r = .41
- Conscientiousness: r = .31
- Reference checks: r = .26
- Job experience (years): r = .18
- Years of education: r = .10

## Best combinations

Because GMA is the primary predictor, the highest-utility strategy is GMA plus a second method that adds incremental validity. The best practical combinations are GMA plus a work sample test (highest validity but costly), GMA plus an integrity test (r = .65), and GMA plus a structured interview (r = .63).

## Anti-pattern rooted in the data

The two signals recruiters lean on most, years of experience (.18) and years of education (.10), are among the weakest predictors of performance, yet resumes are usually screened on exactly those. Unstructured interviews (.38) predict noticeably worse than structured ones (.51). The practical lesson: screen on ability and job-relevant samples, structure the interview, and treat experience and credentials as thresholds rather than as ranking signals.

title: Gallup, State of the Global Workplace (engagement levels and cost)
text:
## The scale of disengagement

Gallup's State of the Global Workplace finds that only about 20% of employees globally are engaged (down from 23% in 2022). Low engagement costs the world economy roughly $10 trillion in lost productivity, equal to about 9% of global GDP.

## Managers are the fulcrum, and they are struggling

Manager engagement fell 9 percentage points since 2022, from 31% to 22%, with a further 5-point decline year over year. In best-practice organizations, 79% of managers are engaged, nearly four times the global average. Leaders also carry a heavier emotional load than individual contributors, reporting higher daily stress (+7 points), anger (+12), sadness (+11), and loneliness (+10).

## Implications for HR

Gallup's data consistently shows that managers account for the majority of the variance in team engagement, so the highest-leverage HR investment is selecting and developing good managers, not adding perks. The anti-pattern is treating engagement as a morale event (parties, swag) rather than as the day-to-day quality of the manager relationship, clear expectations, recognition, development, and the sense that one's work matters.

title: Northern Illinois University CITL, Gagne's Nine Events of Instruction
text:
## Gagne's Nine Events of Instruction

Robert Gagne's nine events map the external instruction to the internal cognitive processes needed for learning. A well-designed lesson moves through all nine.

1. Gain attention. Ensure learners are ready by presenting a stimulus that captures attention: novelty and surprise, thought-provoking questions, or an ice breaker.
2. Inform learners of the objectives. Tell students the outcomes so they know what they are expected to learn and do; describe the required performance and the criteria for a good standard.
3. Stimulate recall of prior learning. Connect new information to existing knowledge or prior experience by asking about previous experiences and relating past content to the current topic.
4. Present the content. Cue and present lesson content using multiple formats (video, demonstration, lecture, group work) and active learning, not a single wall of text.
5. Provide learning guidance. Help students learn how to learn with scaffolding, worked examples and non-examples, mnemonics, concept maps, case studies, and analogies.
6. Elicit performance (practice). Have learners apply the material to reinforce the skill and confirm understanding through activities and formative assessment.
7. Provide feedback. Give timely feedback: confirmatory (encouragement), evaluative (accuracy), remedial (guidance toward the answer), and descriptive (suggestions to improve).
8. Assess performance. Test whether the stated objectives were achieved with pre- and post-tests and objective rubrics.
9. Enhance retention and transfer. Help learners retain and generalize by connecting concepts across the course and having them convert information between formats and apply it to real situations.

## Design implication

Gagne's model is a checklist against the common failure of jumping straight to event 4 (dump content) and skipping attention, objectives, prior-knowledge activation, guided practice, and feedback, the events that actually cause learning to stick.

title: InstructionalDesign.org, The ADDIE Model
text:
## ADDIE: the generic instructional systems design process

ADDIE is the process traditionally used by instructional designers, comprising five phases whose outputs feed the next: Analysis, Design, Development, Implementation, Evaluation.

## Analysis

Clarify the instructional problem and establish learning objectives. Key questions: Who is the audience and what are their characteristics? What is the desired new behavioral outcome? What learning constraints exist? What are the delivery options and timeline?

## Design

Work on learning objectives, assessment instruments, exercises, content, subject-matter analysis, lesson planning, and media selection. Activities include storyboards, user-interface design, prototypes, and applying visual-design principles. Design should be systematic and specific.

## Development

Instructional designers and subject-matter experts assemble content assets; developers integrate technologies; testers debug. This is where the storyboard becomes real material.

## Implementation

Train the facilitators and the learners, ensure materials and tools are available, and confirm the course or application actually works.

## Evaluation

Two components: formative evaluation is present in each of the earlier phases (test and improve as you build), and summative evaluation consists of tests designed for criterion-referenced items plus opportunities for feedback.

## Note and critique

Although each step feeds the next, the sequence need not be strictly linear, and evaluation runs throughout rather than only at the end. The common anti-pattern is treating ADDIE as a rigid waterfall where evaluation is bolted on last: by then it is too late and too expensive to fix a flawed analysis. Agile alternatives such as Michael Allen's Successive Approximation Model (SAM) were created to prototype and evaluate in rapid iterations instead.

title: The Decision Lab, Cognitive Load Theory (John Sweller)
text:
## Cognitive Load Theory

Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), developed by John Sweller in the 1980s, explains why learning breaks down when mental effort exceeds working memory's limited capacity. Working memory was traditionally theorized to hold five to nine bits of information at a time (Miller's 7 plus or minus 2); more recent estimates put it at about four. Long-term memory, by contrast, is effectively unlimited and stores organized schemas. Learning is the process of building and automating those schemas.

## Three types of load

Cognitive load has three additive components. Intrinsic load is the inherent difficulty of the material itself (its element interactivity), and stays relatively constant regardless of how it is presented. Extraneous load is difficulty imposed by poor presentation and instructional-design choices; it does not contribute to learning and can be reduced by better design. Germane load is the productive effort devoted to organizing information into schemas and genuine understanding.

## The design goal

The overarching goal of CLT is to reduce extraneous load, for example by cleaning up cluttered slides and removing distractions, so that freed-up working-memory capacity can be redirected toward germane processing. When intrinsic load is high, designers can also manage it by segmenting content and using pre-training on key terms before the full lesson.

## Anti-pattern

Decorative graphics, background music, on-screen text that duplicates narration, and split-attention layouts (a diagram whose labels are in a separate legend) all pile on extraneous load and depress learning, even though they can make a course look richer. Overloading working memory is the single most common way instruction fails.

title: RetrievalPractice.org (Pooja K. Agarwal), Why Retrieval Practice Works
text:
## Retrieval practice: pulling information out beats putting it in

Retrieval practice is the strategy of bringing information to mind, which enhances and boosts learning. Instead of focusing on getting information into learners' heads through rereading and note-taking, the evidence-based approach emphasizes pulling information out through deliberate recall (low-stakes quizzes, brain dumps, flashcards, free recall).

## The evidence

The page draws on more than 100 years of cognitive-science research showing that significant learning happens during retrieval, not just during initial encoding. Dr. Pooja K. Agarwal's research indicates retrieval practice can increase students' grades from a C to an A. Benefits appear across K-12 through medical school, across subjects from history to CPR skills, across long-term retention over days, weeks, and months, and across all developmental stages.

## Why it works

Three mechanisms: the use it or lose it principle (recall strengthens memory the way practicing an instrument does); desirable difficulty (the effortful struggle of retrieval, not the ease of rereading, is what builds durable memory); and metacognition (retrieval gives students accurate awareness of what they do and do not know).

## Anti-pattern

Rereading and highlighting feel productive and create an illusion of mastery (fluency), but they are among the weakest study strategies. Because retrieval feels harder, learners and instructors wrongly avoid it. Related evidence-based partners are spacing (distributing practice across sessions with growing intervals) and interleaving (mixing related topics rather than blocking one at a time).

title: George Mason University (Dabbagh), Formats for Writing Performance Objectives (ABCD and Mager)
text:
## Writing measurable learning objectives

A learning objective states what a learner will be able to do after instruction, in observable and measurable terms. Two canonical formats dominate instructional design.

## The ABCD format

Four components: Audience (the target learner), Behavior (the observable action to be performed), Condition (the circumstances under which performance occurs), and Degree (the measurable standard of acceptable performance). Example: Using tape-recorded readings (condition), students in drama class (audience) will select (behavior) the proper voice for each character as indicated in the text (degree).

## Mager's three-component format

Robert Mager emphasizes three elements. Performance: an objective always states what a learner is expected to be able to do or produce to be considered competent. Conditions: it describes the important conditions, if any, under which the performance is to occur. Criterion: it describes the criteria of acceptable performance, that is, how well someone must perform to be considered competent. Example: Given a list of thirty-five chemical elements (condition), the learner must be able to recall and write the valences (performance) of at least thirty (criterion).

## Anti-pattern

Both formats demand precise, measurable language. Vague verbs like understand, know, appreciate, or be familiar with cannot be observed or assessed and should be replaced with action verbs (list, calculate, select, write, demonstrate, diagnose) tied to the appropriate Bloom's level. An objective you cannot write a test item for is not a usable objective.

title: eLearning Industry, Action Mapping by Cathy Moore
text:
## Action mapping: design for behavior, not information

Cathy Moore's action mapping is a visual approach that starts from performance rather than content. Its purpose is to solve a business problem by helping people change what they do, not merely to transfer knowledge. The method has four steps.

1. Identify a measurable business goal. Align the training to a concrete organizational objective (for example, reduce support tickets by X, cut safety incidents) so success is measurable and the value is provable.
2. Identify what people need to DO to reach that goal. Break the goal into the specific on-the-job actions people must perform, expressed as observable behaviors, not topics to know.
3. Design practice activities. Create realistic practice that makes learners rehearse each action in a job-like scenario, with consequences and feedback, so they build the skill.
4. Identify the minimum information needed. Provide only the information required to complete each activity. If a piece of content does not support an action, omit it.

## The core critique

Moore challenges the traditional information-dump approach, where courses are built by pouring in everything a subject-matter expert knows. Training should focus on doing rather than content delivery; by supplying only the information necessary for each activity, designers avoid overwhelming learners with extraneous detail. The shift is from generic, content-heavy courses to focused, performance-driven design where every element earns its place by helping learners accomplish a real-world action.

## Anti-pattern

The spray-and-pray course: pages of narrated bullet points followed by a knowledge-check quiz. It feels like training, produces completion certificates, and changes no behavior, because it was never mapped to a business goal or a real action.

title: Kirkpatrick Partners, The Kirkpatrick Model (Four Levels of Evaluation)
text:
## The Kirkpatrick Model: four levels of training evaluation

The Kirkpatrick Model evaluates a learning program across four levels, from immediate reaction to business results.

## Level 1: Reaction

Measures the degree to which participants find the experience favorable, engaging, relevant, and supportive of the work needed to achieve the targeted outcomes. Components: favorability, engagement, relevance, and supportiveness. Relevance is the most predictive measure of whether the learning will actually be applied.

## Level 2: Learning

Measures the degree to which participants acquire the intended knowledge, skills, attitude, confidence, and commitment. Confidence (I believe I can do this on the job) and commitment (I intend to do it) are early predictors of later performance.

## Level 3: Behavior

Measures the degree to which participants apply the critical behaviors on the job and are supported in and held accountable for that performance. Success requires required drivers, the reinforcement, encouragement, accountability, and rewards (manager check-ins, observation, job aids, incentives) that make behavior change stick.

## Level 4: Results

Measures the degree to which targeted organizational outcomes occur as a result of the initiative and the performance support. Uses leading indicators (early signs the behavior is producing the intended effect) and lagging indicators, often drawn from existing organizational metrics.

## Anti-pattern

Most organizations stop at Levels 1 and 2 (a smile sheet and a quiz) because Levels 3 and 4 are harder to measure. But Levels 3 and 4 are where value lives. The New World Kirkpatrick Model recommends starting with Level 4 (the result you want) and designing backward, and building the Level 3 required drivers before training, since roughly the majority of transfer failure is caused by an unsupportive work environment, not a bad course.

title: University of Iowa (Tippie), Merrill's First Principles of Instruction
text:
## Merrill's First Principles of Instruction

David Merrill (2002) reviewed many instructional theories and distilled five principles they share. Learning is promoted when all five are present, and impeded when any is omitted.

1. Task-centered (problem-centered). Design instruction around authentic, real-world problems learners are likely to encounter, and engage them in solving those problems rather than studying abstract topics.
2. Activation. Engage learners' prior knowledge and experience as a foundation for new learning, building connections between what they already know and the new material.
3. Demonstration. Show learners, do not just tell: provide clear models, examples, worked demonstrations, simulations, or case studies of the desired performance.
4. Application. Give learners opportunities to practice and apply the new knowledge and skills in authentic contexts, with feedback and coaching that fades over time.
5. Integration. Promote transfer by having learners connect and apply their learning to new, real-world situations and reflect on, discuss, and defend their new skill.

## The cycle

The principles form a task-centered cycle: starting from a real problem, learners move through activation, demonstration, application, and integration, often across several progressively harder problems. Merrill's insight is that these principles are design-level and theory-agnostic: whatever model or authoring tool you use, effective instruction shows the skill, has learners do the skill on real tasks, and connects it back to their world, rather than presenting information and hoping it transfers.

title: Deans for Impact, Learning Styles: What Does the Research Say?
text:
## The learning-styles myth

A top-1% instructional designer knows that learning styles are a myth. The specific claim being tested is the meshing hypothesis: that students learn more if instruction matches their preferred learning style (visual learners get visual instruction, auditory learners get listening-based instruction).

## The evidence

The rigorous test requires classifying learners by style, randomly assigning them to different instruction methods, and testing all identically; the hypothesis is supported only if different style-groups benefit from different methods. In the landmark review by Pashler, McDaniel, Rohrer, and Bjork (2008) for the Association for Psychological Science, the conclusion was stark: if classification of students' learning styles has practical utility, it remains to be demonstrated. Among the studies examined, only one offered even partial support and two directly contradicted the hypothesis. The American Psychological Association echoed the lack of support in 2019.

## What to do instead

Learners do have preferences about how information is presented, but preference is not the same as improved learning. The better approach is to vary instructional modality based on the demands of the content, not the presumed style of the learner: teach geography with maps and music with sound because the content demands it. Matching to a preferred style can even harm retention, because memory is the residue of thought: when style-matching makes learning feel easy, students engage less deeply and forget faster.

## Anti-pattern

Building or labeling courses around VAK (visual-auditory-kinesthetic) styles, administering learning-styles inventories, and tailoring delivery to them wastes resources that would be better spent on evidence-based practices like retrieval practice, spacing, worked examples, and dual coding.

title: Educational Technology, Mayer's Principles of Multimedia Learning
text:
## Mayer's Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning

Richard Mayer's theory rests on three assumptions. Dual channels: information is processed through two channels, one for visual/pictorial and one for auditory/verbal information. Limited capacity: each channel can handle only a limited amount at once (see cognitive load theory). Active processing: meaningful learning happens when the learner actively selects, organizes, and integrates the material.

## The 12 principles

1. Coherence: exclude irrelevant words, images, and sounds; less is more.
2. Signaling: add cues that highlight the key information and the structure of the material.
3. Redundancy: graphics with narration beat graphics with narration plus on-screen text that duplicates the narration.
4. Spatial contiguity: place related words and images near each other, not far apart.
5. Temporal contiguity: present corresponding words and images at the same time, not successively.
6. Segmenting: break content into learner-controlled, bite-sized segments.
7. Pre-training: teach the names and characteristics of key concepts before the full lesson.
8. Modality: graphics with spoken narration beat graphics with on-screen text.
9. Multimedia: people learn better from words and pictures together than from words alone.
10. Personalization: use a conversational rather than formal style.
11. Voice: a natural human voice beats a machine/synthetic voice.
12. Image: adding a static image of the speaker on screen does not necessarily improve learning.

## Design implication

The principles are unified by cognitive-load management: coherence, redundancy, spatial and temporal contiguity, and signaling reduce extraneous processing; segmenting, pre-training, and modality manage essential processing; multimedia, personalization, voice, and image foster generative processing. The classic anti-pattern is the narrated slide that reads its own on-screen bullets aloud word for word, which violates both redundancy and modality and measurably reduces learning.

title: EBU R 128, Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals
text:
## EBU R 128: the loudness standard

EBU R 128 is the European Broadcasting Union recommendation that shifted audio from peak normalization to loudness normalization. It is built on the ITU-R BS.1770 algorithm, which applies K-weighting (a frequency weighting that approximates how humans perceive loudness) before measuring.

## The numbers

Target Programme Loudness is -23 LUFS. The permitted deviation is +/-0.5 LU in general, widening to +/-1 LU when practical limitations exist (for example live, less-predictable material). The Maximum Permitted True Peak Level is -1 dBTP, measured with a true-peak meter. Loudness Range (LRA) describes the statistical dynamic variation of a programme; R 128 sets no fixed maximum on it.

## Units

LUFS = Loudness Units referenced to Full Scale, an absolute scale where 0 dBFS is digital full scale. LU is a relative unit where 1 LU equals 1 dB; it expresses deviation from the target. So -23 LUFS is an absolute target, and being 2 LU too loud means -21 LUFS.

## Gating

To stop silence from dragging the average down, integrated loudness uses two gates: an absolute gate at -70 LUFS (anything quieter is treated as silence) and a relative gate at -10 LU below the ungated level.

## Three meters

EBU Mode specifies three measurement windows: Momentary (M), a 400 ms sliding window; Short-term (S), a 3 second sliding window; and Integrated (I), the whole programme from start to finish. Real-time meters update at a minimum of 10 Hz (short-term) and 1 Hz (integrated).

## Anti-pattern

Mastering to peaks (normalizing so the loudest sample hits 0 dBFS) does not control perceived loudness and is exactly what R 128 replaced: two files can both peak at 0 dBFS yet differ wildly in loudness. Ignoring true peak and normalizing to -1 dBFS (sample peak) still allows inter-sample peaks to clip on playback.

title: Podnews, How to do loudness: the LUFS and LKFS FAQ for podcasters
text:
## Loudness targets for podcasts

The podcast industry has mostly standardised on -16 LUFS integrated for stereo files, which is the level Apple Podcasts asks for. For mono files the equivalent target is -19 LUFS (a mono file measures about 3 LU quieter than the same material summed to stereo, so -19 LUFS mono lands at roughly -16 LUFS when played back). True peak should not exceed -1 dB True Peak (-1 dBTP).

## LUFS vs peak

LUFS is a measurement of loudness over a period of time, and a perceptual measurement (how loud does this sound to your ears), not a measure of peak electrical energy like the older PPM or VU meters. That is why two files with identical peaks can sound very different in loudness.

## Why normalize

For podcasting, loudness normalization ensures that if you play five podcasts back to back, they all sound equally loud and the listener never has to reach for the volume control. Consistency across episodes and across shows is the whole point.

## Platform targets

Music streaming platforms normalize to their own targets: Spotify and YouTube request approximately -14 LUFS, while most podcasters still deliver -16 LUFS. If you master too loud (for example -9 LUFS), the platform simply turns you down, so you gain crushed dynamics and no extra loudness.

## Anti-pattern

Over-compressing and limiting a spoken-word episode to be as loud as possible is self-defeating: the platform loudness-normalizes it back down, and you are left with fatiguing, lifeless audio. Aim for the target loudness with natural dynamics rather than maximum loudness.

title: The Podcast Standards Project, Audio (de facto delivery standard)
text:
## The de facto podcast audio delivery standard

The Podcast Standards Project documents what podcasts actually ship, giving a practical target for encoding a finished episode.

## Loudness and peak

The most common loudness target is -16 LUFS integrated, which is what Apple Podcasts recommends; a meaningful share of podcasts also use -18 LUFS. Apple recommends a true peak of -1 dBTP, although in practice many podcasts leave true peak at 0 dBTP (which risks inter-sample clipping on lossy playback).

## Format and bitrate

MP3 is dominant, used by essentially 100% of podcasts, because it plays everywhere. The most common bitrate is 256 kbps (about 60% of shows), with 128 kbps a distant second (about 10%). AAC/M4A is supported by major platforms but almost never used as the delivery format. The majority of episodes are stereo (about 64%), though spoken-word content is often better served by mono to halve the file size at the same perceived quality.

## Practical takeaway

A safe, broadly compatible spoken-word export is an MP3 at 128 kbps (mono) or higher, normalized to -16 LUFS with true peak at or below -1 dBTP. Music-heavy shows justify a higher bitrate and stereo.

## Anti-pattern

Delivering a very high-bitrate stereo WAV or a 320 kbps stereo MP3 for a two-voice talk show wastes listeners' bandwidth and storage for no audible benefit; conversely, a 64 kbps file makes voices sound swirly and thin.

title: Transom.org, The Basics (field recording and interviewing craft)
text:
## Recording levels in the field

Aim for a healthy record level, roughly 5 to 8 on a typical mic input knob: high enough to sit well above the recorder's electronic noise, but low enough that peaks never clip. Clipping in the field is unrecoverable, so leave headroom and watch the meters.

## Microphone technique

Keep the mic close, about six inches from the speaker's mouth, and slightly off-axis (to the side) to avoid plosives, the pops from P and B sounds hitting the capsule. Move in for soft talkers and back off for loud laughter. Close-miking is what separates broadcast-quality voice from thin, roomy audio.

## Kill the noise before you record

Listen for interfering sounds and deal with them at the source: air conditioners, fluorescent lights, refrigerators, traffic, and radios. Turn them off or move away rather than hoping to fix it later. Always monitor on headphones so you catch wind noise, handling noise, and cable rustle while you can still do something about it.

## Capture room tone and ambience

Record a stretch of room tone (the sound of the space with no one talking) at every location; you will need it to patch edits later. Grab the sundry sounds of the scene too, phones ringing, dogs barking, clocks ticking, from varied distances, to give the editor material to build a sense of place.

## Interview technique

Get people to show you, not just tell you: have them describe where you are and what they are doing, and keep them moving. It relaxes the subject, builds immediacy, and captures varied acoustics.

## Anti-pattern

Recording hot with no headphones, mic held far away and dead-on-axis, in an untreated noisy room, produces audio no amount of post can rescue. The fix is upstream: levels, distance, off-axis angle, and killing noise at the source.

title: iZotope RX 11 Documentation, Spectral De-noise
text:
## Spectral De-noise: learn a profile, then subtract it

Spectral De-noise removes tonal and broadband noise (tape hiss, HVAC, outdoor ambience, line noise, ground loops, camera motors, fans, wind, complex buzz) by learning a spectral profile of the noise and subtracting it wherever a signal's energy drops below that profile.

## The Learn workflow

Before learning, select the longest possible noise-only section, ideally a few seconds, that contains only the noise you want to remove and none of the content you want to keep. Such sections are usually found at the start or end of a file or in a pause between words. Then press Learn to capture the noise fingerprint.

## Tonal vs broadband

The module automatically separates noise into tonal parts (hum, buzz, interference: steady harmonic content) and random/broadband parts (hiss), and gives each its own reduction control so you can suppress each type independently.

## Reduction and artifacts

The Reduction slider sets suppression depth in dB, but strong suppression also degrades low-level signal, so apply only as much as you need. The Artifact Control parameter trades between spectral subtraction (more accurate but can sound chirpy) and gating (fewer chirps but a noisier envelope).

## Anti-pattern: over-processing

The classic mistake is pushing reduction too hard to chase a dead-silent background. This introduces watery, chirpy, underwater artifacts (musical noise) and hollows out the voice, which sounds worse than a little honest hiss. Reduce gently, and if the noise floor is bad, fix it at the source instead. Learn the profile from true noise only: if your selection includes speech, you will subtract part of the voice.

title: iZotope Learn, Gain Staging: What It Is and How to Do It
text:
## What gain staging is

Gain staging is the process of making sure audio is at an optimal level for the next processor in the chain, to minimize noise and distortion. Every stage (mic preamp, interface, DAW track, plugins, master bus) has an ideal operating level, and getting each one right keeps the signal clean end to end.

## The reference level

The sweet spot for most analog-modeled plugins is around -18 dBFS average, which corresponds to the classic analog standard of 0 VU. Engineers commonly set individual tracks to peak around -18 to -20 dBFS at unity fader position, leaving headroom as plugins accumulate through the chain.

## Why it matters

The hard digital ceiling is 0 dBFS. Exceeding it causes hard digital clipping, which squares off the waveform and is destructive and permanent when exported to fixed-point (16- or 24-bit) files. Analog-modeled processors are also designed to distort when pushed too hard, so feeding them a signal that is far too hot changes their tone even below 0 dBFS.

## Practical method

Set a healthy tracking level with headroom, then keep average levels near -18 dBFS through the chain rather than letting each plugin add gain until the master clips. Use a trim/gain utility at the top of a channel to bring a hot source back to the reference before processing.

## Anti-pattern

Recording or mixing with everything slammed near 0 dBFS leaves no headroom, drives analog-modeled plugins into unintended distortion, and risks clipping on export. Recording far too quiet is the opposite error: it buries the voice in the noise floor and forces heavy make-up gain that raises hiss.

title: iZotope Learn, What Is Audio Compression?
text:
## What compression does

Compression controls dynamic range by reducing a signal's level when it rises above a set threshold. It does not make audio louder by itself; it reduces the distance between the loudest and quietest moments, after which make-up gain can raise the whole thing. For spoken voice this evens out a performer who drifts near and far from the mic and keeps quiet words audible against loud ones.

## The parameters

Threshold: the level (in dBFS) at which compression starts; signal above it is compressed, signal below is untouched. Ratio: how hard the excess is reduced. A 4:1 ratio means for every 4 dB above the threshold at the input, only 1 dB above threshold comes out. Higher ratios mean more gain reduction. Attack: how fast the compressor clamps down after the signal crosses the threshold, from very fast (0.1 to 5 ms) to slow (10 to 100 ms). Release: how fast it lets go after the signal falls back below threshold (very fast 0.1 to 5 ms up to 50 ms or longer). Knee: hard knee for abrupt onset, soft knee for a gradual, more transparent onset. Makeup gain: raises the output to compensate for the level lost to compression.

## A dialogue starting point

For smoothing vocal or dialogue dynamics, a common starting point is a medium attack around 8 ms, a medium-to-slow release around 200 ms, and a moderate ratio around 3:1, adjusted so you see only about 3 to 6 dB of gain reduction on the loudest moments while quiet passages stay untouched.

## Anti-pattern

Too high a ratio with too fast an attack squashes every transient flat and pumps audibly; heavy make-up gain then raises the noise floor and any room tone. Over-compressed voice sounds lifeless and fatiguing. Compress a little, and reach for gentle 3 to 6 dB reduction rather than double-digit gain reduction on speech.

title: iZotope Learn, 7 Tips for Using Subtractive EQ When Mixing Audio
text:
## Subtractive EQ: cut problems rather than boost

Subtractive EQ is a decrease in a frequency band's amplitude, that is, a cut. Rather than boosting the frequencies you like, you remove the ones causing problems, which tends to sound more natural and adds less phase and level buildup than piling on boosts.

## Finding the problem frequency

Use the boost-and-sweep method: temporarily boost a narrow band and sweep it across the spectrum until the offending resonance jumps out (nasal honk, boxy mud, harsh whistle), then pull that band down. A spectrum analyzer helps you see what you are targeting.

## Q and amount

Use a narrow Q (around 12) to notch out a specific resonance like a nasal or whistling tone, and a broad Q (around 1) for gentle tonal shaping across a wider range. Keep cuts modest: 2 to 4 dB is often enough, and cutting 6 dB or more tends to sound thin and lifeless and can introduce artifacts.

## Common voice moves

High-pass to remove low-end rumble below roughly 80 to 100 Hz; reduce muddiness in the 200 to 500 Hz range with a fairly narrow cut; presence lives around 3 to 5 kHz and air around 10 to 15 kHz. Reach for dynamic EQ when a static cut sounds too obvious, so the cut only engages when the problem frequency peaks.

## Anti-pattern

Making many aggressive cuts in a row without listening between them produces a hollow, over-processed, bloodless sound. Make one cut, listen, and stop. Over-cutting the low mids to fight mud will also thin the natural body of the voice.

title: iZotope RX, De-ess (removing sibilance)
text:
## De-essing: taming sibilance

RX's De-ess module attenuates sibilance, the harsh, high-frequency spoken sounds that come from S, F, X, SH, and a soft C. Sibilance concentrates in the upper frequencies (commonly the several-kHz region of the voice) and becomes harsh after compression and presence-boosting EQ, which raise those very frequencies.

## Two modes

Classic mode detects sibilants and attenuates them with a broadband gain envelope, ducking the whole signal briefly when an ess occurs. Spectral mode is more transparent and frequency-specific: it attenuates only the high frequencies where sibilance is most active and leaves the lower frequencies untouched, so the body of the voice is preserved while the ess is softened.

## Best practice

A de-esser should engage only on the sibilant moments and only on the sibilant band. Set the threshold so it reacts to harsh esses but ignores normal speech, and apply the minimum reduction that tames the harshness. Because presence EQ and compression aggravate sibilance, place de-essing thoughtfully in the chain (often after the compression that provoked it).

## Anti-pattern

A broadband de-esser set too aggressively lisps the voice: every S turns to a dull TH and the vocal loses its top-end sparkle. The fix is to de-ess narrowly and lightly (spectral mode where available), rather than clamping the entire high end whenever an ess appears. Chasing sibilance with a static high-shelf cut is worse still, since it dulls the whole track, not just the esses.

title: iZotope, What Is a True Peak Limiter?
text:
## True peak limiting

A true peak limiter is a brick-wall limiter that uses oversampling to follow and control the actual analog peak level, not just the digital sample values. A limiter is effectively a compressor with an extremely high (near-infinite) ratio that prevents any signal from crossing its ceiling.

## Inter-sample peaks

True peaks occur between digital samples, so a waveform whose samples read, say, -4 dBFS can actually peak at -1 dBTP once reconstructed by the D/A converter, a 3 dB difference. Pathological signals can show a true peak more than 7 dB above the highest sample value. This is why a file that never exceeds 0 dBFS on a sample meter can still clip the converter or a lossy codec on playback.

## dBTP vs dBFS

dBFS is the peak level of the digital samples (what most DAW meters show). dBTP (decibels True Peak) estimates the analog output level after conversion. Loudness standards specify true-peak ceilings for this reason.

## Ceilings

Keep true peaks below 0 dBFS. A common choice is the -1 to -0.3 dBTP range; EBU R128 mandates -1 dBTP. When the audio will be encoded to a lossy format (MP3, AAC), leave more room (for example -1 to -2 dBTP) because the encoder introduces its own overshoot.

## Anti-pattern

Mastering to a 0 dBFS ceiling on a sample-peak limiter (ignoring true peak) leaves inter-sample overs that distort after D/A conversion and after lossy encoding. Also, true-peak limiting requires slightly more gain reduction than sample limiting and naturally softens transients, so slamming a track into a true-peak brickwall for maximum loudness dulls and pumps it.

title: Castos, Acoustic Treatment for Podcasting (control reverb and reflections)
text:
## Soundproofing vs acoustic treatment

These are different jobs. Soundproofing means structural work to stop sound getting in or out, which is expensive and usually unnecessary for podcasters. Acoustic treatment changes how sound behaves inside the room, and it is what actually improves your recordings.

## Reverb and reflections

Reverb happens when sound bounces off hard surfaces and reaches the mic multiple times, smearing the voice. It is always easier to prevent reflections than to fix them in post. Identify the reflection points (walls, ceiling, floor, desk, window, mirror) and treat them.

## Absorption vs diffusion

Absorption places soft/absorptive material between the sound source and the reflective surface so sound energy dissipates instead of bouncing back. Diffusion uses surfaces of varied depths and angles to scatter reflections, breaking up distinct echoes while keeping a natural room feel. Thicker absorptive material performs better, especially toward lower frequencies; thin foam only absorbs highs. Corners benefit from bass traps.

## Practical, cheap wins

Soft furnishings work: curtains, rugs, upholstered furniture, and heavy blankets draped over reflection points. A furnished room already absorbs and diffuses far better than an empty one, which is why a well-stuffed closet is a classic budget vocal booth. A reflection filter behind the mic and a dynamic mic (less sensitive to the room than a condenser) both reduce captured room sound. Use the mirror test to place panels at first-reflection points, and mic close so direct sound dominates the reflections.

## Anti-pattern

Trying to fix a boomy, echoey room with reverb-removal plugins after the fact rarely sounds clean; treat the room and mic technique first. Buying thin acoustic foam and expecting it to stop low-frequency boom or to soundproof against a neighbor is a common misunderstanding: foam absorbs highs and does not block transmission.
